claims.text: The target material is an as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy alloy in nanoscale thin-film or patterned-nanoribbon form.
The as-deposited nanoscale material has significant interfacial strain.
The as-deposited nanoscale material has a high density of nanoscale defects.
Finite-size-induced interfacial strain largely governs the magnetocaloric response and low-field hysteresis of nanoscale FeMnNiGeSi alloys.
Defect-induced domain-wall pinning largely governs the magnetocaloric response and low-field hysteresis of nanoscale FeMnNiGeSi alloys.
A controlled post-deposition anneal will relax interfacial strain.
Post-deposition annealing will reduce defect density and domain-wall pinning sites.
Reducing strain and pinning sites will produce smoother magnetic-domain motion.
Smoother domain motion after annealing will reduce hysteretic losses and produce a narrower hysteresis loop than in the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing will enhance the magnetic entropy change or adiabatic temperature change relative to the as-deposited baseline.
The annealed nanoscale material's magnetocaloric response will remain lower than that of bulk forms.
The predicted improvements will be most observable at lower cycling frequencies, where heat-transfer limitations do not dominate.
Heat-transfer limitations set the usable magnetic-cooling cycle-frequency range in the nanoscale system.
Relaxing strain reduces thermal gradients, making nanoscale heat-transfer limitations less critical.
The hypothesis applies only when initial strain and defect levels are sufficiently large to influence magnetic-domain dynamics.
Annealed and unannealed specimens should be compared under identical applied fields and cycling frequencies.
Failure of annealing to produce both a statistically significant decrease in hysteresis-loop area and an improved magnetocaloric response would falsify the proposed mechanism.
